Below is an evidence-backed synthesis of how retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems transform human citation patterns and how the epistemic quality of AI-synthesized research compares to human-authored literature reviews.

Introduction and scope
RAG systems embed retrieval into the loop of synthesis, changing not only what is cited but how citations are found, attached to text, organized, and verified. We examine concrete changes to citation practices and evaluate impacts on accuracy, comprehensiveness, novelty, bias, and replicability relative to human-authored literature reviews. <cite id="493b1495-0">Recent frameworks explicitly decompose literature-review writing into reference generation (with required title, authors, venue, and page metadata), abstract writing, and review composition with inline citations to newly generated references</cite>. <cite id="493b1495-1">RAG-powered systems also cluster papers and produce structured reviews with annotated text linked to citations for end-user validation</cite>.

How RAG transforms human citation patterns
1) From manual curation to automated reference recommendation and inline grounding
- RAG pipelines can recommend references directly from a topic, producing structured metadata and requiring models to “cite truth studies” proportionally to claims in the review. <cite id="493b1495-0">Reference generation prompts models to find N most relevant studies with full metadata (title, authors, journal, year, volume, first/last page)</cite>. <cite id="493b1495-0">Review composition tasks then demand that models include N citations aligned with claims to support the review’s content</cite>. 
- In practice, systems integrate clustering and inductive summarization over a selected set of papers, writing an introduction, body with headings, and conclusion, while annotating analytical text with hyperlinked citations that enable on-demand validation. <cite id="493b1495-1">A RAG report generator clusters dozens of papers, structures a comprehensive review, and links analytical text with hyperlinks serving as citations for reference verification</cite>.
- Across disciplines, models show variable skill at recommending reliable references. <cite id="493b1495-2">Hallucinated references remain a prevalent issue and performance varies by discipline</cite>. <cite id="493b1495-3">Relying on Semantic Scholar APIs for verification helps standardize checks, though incomplete retrieval can persist</cite>.

2) Granularity and provenance: more frequent in-text grounding and verifiable bibliographies
- RAG shifts citations from sparse end-lists to dense, claim-aligned anchors. <cite id="493b1495-0">For a 1000-word review, models are prompted to include newly generated citations matching the number of claims</cite>. <cite id="493b1495-1">Each analytical sentence is annotated with clickable citations, and a validation-friendly bibliography is produced at the end</cite>.
- This creates tighter provenance: reviewers can click-through from a statement to its supporting passage and metadata. <cite id="493b1495-1">Hyperlinked citations facilitate immediate reference validation and user verification</cite>.

3) Organization and search orchestration: clustering, re-ranking, and iterative retrieval
- RAG systems leverage clustering and plan-based retrieval strategies to structure synthesis. <cite id="493b1495-1">Clustering capabilities and inductive summarization are used to form coherent sections and headings</cite>. <cite id="493b1495-4">Plan-based prompting and RAG techniques improve paper re-ranking and reduce hallucinations in LLM-assisted literature reviews, though retrieval remains incomplete and requires new querying strategies</cite>.
- Tooling around “LLM agents” for literature review has proliferated, integrating retrieval and critique loops. <cite id="493b1495-4">Tools like DeepResearch and AI Co-Scientist demonstrate improved literature review generation and citation accuracy through enhanced retrieval strategies</cite>.

4) Metadata completeness and verification infrastructure
- RAG pipelines can enforce standardized citation fields and link claims to passages, aiding downstream checking. <cite id="493b1495-0">Required metadata for each recommendation and citation (title, authors, venue, year, volume, pages) increases bibliographic completeness</cite>. <cite id="493b1495-3">Automated checks (e.g., Semantic Scholar API) improve consistency, though minor discrepancies and incomplete retrieval can occur</cite>.

Failure modes that reshape citation behavior
- Despite RAG, hallucinations persist in references and in-situ claims. <cite id="493b1495-2">Hallucinated references remain prevalent across models, and performance differs by discipline</cite>. <cite id="493b1495-4">Even with plan-based prompting and attribution from extracted content, hallucinations are reduced but not eliminated</cite>.
- Coverage gaps and re-ranking weaknesses undermine comprehensive citation. <cite id="493b1495-4">Retrieving all relevant papers consistent with a human review requires new querying strategies; debate-style prompting with attribution improves re-ranking but doesn’t fully solve selection bias</cite>.

Epistemic quality of AI-synthesized reviews vs. human-authored literature reviews
1) Accuracy and factual consistency
- RAG improves fidelity relative to ungrounded generation but does not remove errors. <cite id="493b1495-2">Factual consistency and semantic coverage of generated abstracts and reviews are evaluated against human-written context; hallucinated references remain a common issue</cite>. <cite id="493b1495-4">Plan-based prompting and attribution reduce hallucinations, yet they persist</cite>.
- Evaluations show that high lexical similarity does not guarantee substantive accuracy. <cite id="efb86586-1">LLMs overemphasize positive feedback, lack critical depth, and neglect substance and clarity despite high ROUGE/BERTScore overlap with human reviews</cite>. <cite id="efb86586-0">Novelty assessments can align with human judgments on specific claims, reasoning, prior-work engagement, and depth, but evaluation remains challenging due to subjectivity and knowledge dependence</cite>.
- Head-to-head comparisons with expert-written content suggest mixed outcomes. <cite id="a01522fa-2">A dual-baseline framework compared Qwen2-7b/72b and Claude3.5Sonnet reviews to peer-reviewed Q1 reviews using the same cited literature fragments; evaluations segment reviews into 89 semantic fragments and compare quality with human baselines</cite>. <cite id="efb86586-1">Automated metrics emphasize similarity and informativeness, while newer “LLM-as-judge” approaches add interpretability but still risk black-box evaluation</cite>.

2) Comprehensiveness and coverage
- RAG systems can accelerate coverage of large corpora but may miss key works. <cite id="493b1495-4">LLMs show promising re-ranking and generation but still require improved strategies to retrieve all relevant papers aligned with a human review</cite>. <cite id="493b1495-1">Productized RAG pipelines cluster and summarize dozens of papers into a structured review, speeding comprehension of large volumes</cite>.
- The quality of coverage depends on retrieval quality. <cite id="493b1495-3">Incomplete or inconsistent reference retrieval (e.g., due to depending on Semantic Scholar vs. Google Scholar) can bias the reference list</cite>.

3) Novelty, selection, and bias
- RAG-assisted novelty assessment can match human granularity on specific claims but lacks holistic perspective. <cite id="a01522fa-0">LLM-RAG systems like OpenScholar are used for novelty validation, but critiques note that they provide generic comparisons rather than granular analysis across methodology, problem formulation, and evaluation approaches</cite>. <cite id="a01522fa-0">No prior work has specifically evaluated LLM performance on novelty assessment as a dedicated task; the LLM-as-Judge approach is adopted to align with human novelty judgments</cite>.
- LLM-generated reviews exhibit systematic emphasis differences and can under-criticize weaknesses. <cite id="a01522fa-1">Comparisons of human and LLM reviews show both emphasize “novelty of study design” as a strength and rarely criticize novelty as a weakness; humans highlight presentation clarity more often, while LLMs focus on technical implementation and empirical rigor</cite>. <cite id="efb86586-1">LLMs tend to give overly positive feedback, lack critical depth, and overlook substance/clarity, despite high lexical similarity</cite>.
- Bias and representational risks persist. <cite id="efb86586-4">Automated survey generation can democratize access and accelerate synthesis but may perpetuate biases present in training data or paper databases, potentially overrepresenting certain perspectives and underrepresenting marginalized voices</cite>.

4) Replicability, traceability, and documentation
- RAG improves traceability by linking claims to passages and standardizing metadata. <cite id="493b1495-1">Reviews embed clickable citations that allow readers to validate references and verify statements directly in the text</cite>. <cite id="493b1495-0">Required citation metadata (title, authors, journal, volume, pages) enhances bibliographic traceability</cite>.
- However, persistent hallucinations and retrieval incompleteness erode replicability. <cite id="493b1495-2">Hallucinated references are prevalent despite evaluation efforts</cite>. <cite id="493b1495-4">Retrieval gaps and plan-based limitations mean outputs can still mis-cite or omit key evidence</cite>.

5) Human-judge comparisons and reliability
- Agreement between AI evaluators and humans is moderate-to-low and context-dependent. <cite id="a01522fa-4">AI reviewer and human reviewer agreement in quality assessments was 22%, with similar agreement levels for AI vs. human pairs and human vs. human pairs; AI ratings were biased, favoring higher quality abstracts</cite>. <cite id="a01522fa-2">LLM-as-judge methods can reach high consistency with human reviewers for certain criteria (e.g., civility: perfect agreement; relevance: near-perfect), yet position, length, and self-bias can persist and must be mitigated by design</cite>.
- Reviews can be structured to reduce bias and improve transparency. <cite id="a01522fa-2">A dual-baseline evaluation compares model-generated reviews to expert-written reviews using identical literature fragments, enabling quantitative benchmarking and statistical validation</cite>.

Headline findings: where RAG improves vs. degrades epistemic quality
- Improvements relative to ungrounded LLM writing:
  • Traceability and verification: embedded, clickable citations and standardized metadata make it easier to validate claims and sources. <cite id="493b1495-1">Analytical text is annotated with hyperlinks serving as citations, and a bibliography supports reference validation</cite>. <cite id="493b1495-0">Citations must include full bibliographic metadata to support claims</cite>.
  • Speed and coverage: clustering and retrieval pipelines compress synthesis over large corpora and suggest relevant references from a topic. <cite id="493b1495-1">A RAG system generates a report over a selection of papers, clustering and summarizing to expedite comprehension</cite>. <cite id="493b1495-0">Reference generation tasks evaluate models’ ability to recommend reliable studies for a given topic</cite>.
  • Reduced hallucination risk vs. human-written baselines: plan-based prompting and RAG reduce but do not eliminate hallucinations; evaluators note improved re-ranking and in-line attribution. <cite id="493b1495-4">Plan-based prompting and attribution from extracted content improve re-ranking and reduce hallucinations</cite>. <cite id="493b1495-2">Across models, hallucinated references remain prevalent; discipline-specific performance varies</cite>.
  • Structured organization: headings and coherent sections produced by clustering improve navigability. <cite id="493b1495-1">LLM clustering structures introduction, body, and conclusion with pertinent headings</cite>.
- Degrations and risks:
  • Omitted or hallucinated references: despite verification APIs, errors in reference lists and claim grounding undermine trust. <cite id="493b1495-2">Hallucinated references are a prevalent issue</cite>. <cite id="493b1495-3">Precise metadata and incomplete retrieval can bias the reference set</cite>.
  • Shallow critique and positive bias: LLM-critique modules often miss substance and clarity, give overly positive ratings, and under-emphasize presentation issues relative to humans. <cite id="efb86586-1">LLMs overemphasize positive feedback, lack critical depth, and neglect substance/clarity</cite>. <cite id="a01522fa-1">LLMs focus more on technical implementation and empirical rigor than humans focus on clarity</cite>.
  • Selection bias and novelty assessment gaps: RAG can miss nuanced novelty across methods and problem formulations; generic comparisons may substitute for granular analysis. <cite id="a01522fa-0">LLM-RAG novelty tools provide generic comparisons rather than granular analysis across methodological axes</cite>.
  • Systemic bias and representational risks: automated synthesis can perpetuate biases in training corpora and databases. <cite id="efb86586-4">Automated surveys risk perpetuating biases, overrepresenting certain perspectives and underrepresenting marginalized voices</cite>.
  • Reliability limits in screening and evaluation: AI ratings can be biased and less reliable for low-quality items; agreement with humans is modest. <cite id="a01522fa-4">AI quality ratings show systematic bias and only 22% agreement with human assessments, with similar agreement levels to human-human pairs</cite>.

Mechanisms, trade-offs, and guardrails
- Retrieval orchestration and plan management: hybrid pipelines that combine embedding-based search, citation-grounded critique, and debate-style re-ranking reduce hallucinations and improve ranking. <cite id="493b1495-4">Debate prompting with attribution based on extracted content improves re-ranking; plan-based RAG reduces hallucinations but does not eliminate them</cite>.
- Evaluation frameworks and transparency: multi-dimensional metrics (novelty claim alignment, reasoning alignment, prior-work engagement, depth) and LLM-as-judge methods help surface gaps; rolling evaluations on recent arXiv corpora keep pace with fast-evolving literature. <cite id="efb86586-0">An LLM-as-Judge framework aligns AI novelty assessments with human-style judgments across claim alignment, reasoning alignment, prior-work engagement, and depth of analysis</cite>. <cite id="efb86586-1">ReviewEval emphasizes interpretable metrics beyond similarity, addressing black-box evaluation pitfalls</cite>. <cite id="493b1495-4">A rolling evaluation on recent arXiv papers shows RAG-assisted pipelines are promising but still require stronger retrieval strategies</cite>.
- Verification infrastructure: enforce citation metadata, link claims to passages, and integrate open citation graphs. <cite id="493b1495-0">Mandating full citation fields for generated references improves metadata completeness</cite>. <cite id="493b1495-1">Clickable citations in the text and end-of-review bibliographies enable immediate validation</cite>.
- Human-in-the-loop guardrails: clearly label AI-generated content, add disclaimers, and perform post-hoc fact-checking; use dual-baseline comparisons to human Q1 reviews for the same literature set. <cite id="efb86586-4">AI-generated surveys should be labeled to maintain academic transparency; quality and bias concerns require attention</cite>. <cite id="a01522fa-2">Dual-baseline evaluations compare model reviews to expert-written content using identical literature fragments for rigorous benchmarking</cite>.
- Data integrity and leakage: update test corpora regularly and adopt leakage-mitigating leaderboards. <cite id="493b1495-3">Relying on Semantic Scholar improves consistency; LLM-generated outputs often have minor discrepancies; to address rapid model iteration, deploy rolling leaderboards with live test updates</cite>.

Practical implications for researchers and institutions
- Workflows: combine embedding search with citation-grounded critique, and use debate-style re-ranking to improve selection and reduce hallucinations; annotate every claim with a linkable citation and standard metadata; maintain a verifiable bibliography. <cite id="493b1495-4">Plan-based prompting with attribution improves re-ranking and reduces hallucinations</cite>. <cite id="493b1495-1">Embedding clustering plus inductive summarization with clickable citations yields structured, verifiable reports</cite>.
- Guardrails: run automated fact-check passes, use Semantic Scholar-backed verification, and adopt LLM-as-judge evaluations for novelty, substance, and clarity; disclose AI assistance and label AI-generated artifacts. <cite id="493b1495-3">SemScholar-backed checks standardize verification but may miss some references</cite>. <cite id="efb86586-1">LLM-as-judge and interpretable metrics address black-box issues in AI review evaluation</cite>. <cite id="efb86586-4">Clear labeling prevents academic misrepresentation</cite>.
- Expectations: RAG significantly accelerates synthesis and improves traceability and initial accuracy relative to ungrounded models, but human oversight remains essential to control selection bias, ensure critical depth, and uphold academic integrity. <cite id="493b1495-0">Reference generation and citation-backed composition tasks make LLMs effective copilots for finding and citing relevant studies</cite>. <cite id="efb86586-1">Despite high similarity to human reviews, AI reviews often lack critical depth and focus too much on positives</cite>. <cite id="493b1495-2">Discipline-specific performance and prevalent hallucinated references underscore the need for guardrails</cite>.

Summary
RAG systems transform citation from a post-hoc bibliography task into an integral, interactive part of argumentation: claims are densely grounded with linkable passages and complete metadata, and synthesis is organized via clustering and retrieval. <cite id="493b1495-1">Reviews now include clickable citations enabling immediate validation and structured sections created by clustering</cite>. <cite id="493b1495-0">Reference generation tasks embed full bibliographic details and force proportional grounding of claims</cite>. Epistemically, these changes improve traceability, speed, and baseline accuracy compared to ungrounded LLM outputs, but they also introduce new risks—hallucinated or incomplete references, positive and technical-focus biases, and potential perpetuation of systemic biases—requiring rigorous evaluation frameworks and human oversight. <cite id="493b1495-2">Hallucinated references persist across models and vary by discipline</cite>. <cite id="efb86586-1">LLM reviews can mirror human structure yet miss substance and critical depth</cite>. <cite id="a01522fa-1">LLM emphasis on implementation and rigor can skew attention away from clarity and presentation</cite>. <cite id="efb86586-4">Automated synthesis may amplify database biases unless carefully audited</cite>. Overall, RAG improves replicability and accelerates synthesis, but relative to human-authored literature reviews it often achieves comparable accuracy with better traceability yet comparable or lower critical depth unless augmented with strong retrieval orchestration, plan-based prompting, and human-in-the-loop verification. <cite id="493b1495-4">Plan-based RAG reduces hallucinations but not completely, and better retrieval strategies are needed to capture all relevant works</cite>. <cite id="a01522fa-2">Dual-baseline comparisons to expert-written reviews with identical literature show that careful design can make AI reviews competitive on quality criteria while making biases and limitations explicit</cite>.

Strategy #6 is meta-level and could expose inability to critique methodology, but risks being too philosophical. I'll go with #5 as it's concrete yet extremely demanding.

Below we decompose how specific computational elements inside Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) architectures causally shift what, how often, and how reliably models cite sources, and we separate mechanisms with empirical evidence from those that are theoretically proposed but remain under-validated.

# Background: What “citation patterns” and mechanisms mean in RAG

RAG introduces external retrieval and generation loops that trace claims to documents, creating three interacting levers that determine citation behavior: (1) retrieval and selection (which documents/paragraphs are brought into context), (2) fusion and decoding (how the generator binds claims to specific sources, including whether and how citations are produced during decoding), and (3) training and control signals (whether models are tuned to add, remove, or refine citations before final generation). <cite id="6d1bc0cf-0">RAG augments LLMs with retrieval to reduce hallucinations and produce citation-backed synthesis, with many systems integrating retrieval mechanisms, full-text grounding, and multi-stage filtering to improve factual accuracy and contextual relevance</cite>.

# Mechanisms with empirical evidence of impact on citation patterns

1) Retrieval quality and reranking determine which sources are exposed to the generator

- Causal evidence: Systems that swap dense/sparse or add rerankers show improved retrieval precision and context-aware citation generation, demonstrating that better retrieval causally increases the likelihood that relevant, timely, and authoritative sources are cited. <cite id="6e9c7dbb-0">A multi-level hybrid RAG approach improves both retrieval precision and context-aware citation generation compared to single-level methods, with a full toolkit for end-to-end evaluation</cite>.

2) Full-text grounding and fine-grained citation generation shift topical and evidentiary specificity
- Mechanism and effect: Using full-text passages (not only abstracts) and generating citation sentences around specific context spans enables precise, claim-aligned citations. <cite id="b58d326c-0">Citation text generation concatenates target citation context with retrieved Cited Text Spans (CTS) and uses Fusion-in-Decoder with BART to align claims to specific source spans</cite>. <cite id="6d1bc0cf-0">Using CTS instead of abstracts for grounding improves citation accuracy and avoids hallucinations, highlighting the importance of full-text integration</cite>. <cite id="b58d326c-2">FiD reads long inputs from multiple documents and supports generating citation sentences that reference multiple documents</cite>.
- Causal evidence: Models grounded on CTS and fine-grained references show improved attributional faithfulness compared to abstract-only retrieval, indicating that moving to full-text grounding changes the distribution of citations toward more specific, directly supported claims and entities. <cite id="6d1bc0cf-0">Full-text grounding with CTS reduces hallucinations and improves contextual relevance for citation-backed synthesis</cite>. <cite id="b58d326c-3">The decoder attends over encoder blocks representing citing and cited papers and supports multiple citations with controlled intents (background, method, supportive, not_supportive), enabling more nuanced citation patterns</cite>.

3) Instruction-tuned and in-generation attribution mechanisms alter how often and how tightly citations are attached
- Mechanism and effect: Two paradigms—simultaneous generation with prompt/intent tuning and post-hoc attribution—change when and how citations are inserted. <cite id="b58d326c-1">Simultaneous, prompt-guided citation inclusion (e.g., P-ICL, instruction tuning) produces single-pass attributions but relies on the model parsing prompt formats; post-hoc attribution first generates citation-free text then traces sources from hidden states/attention, offering interpretability at extra cost</cite>. C$^2$-Cite strengthens the semantic tie between citation markers and content within a single pass. <cite id="b58d326c-1">C$^2$-Cite is an instruction-tuned attribution method that retains single-pass efficiency while improving the intrinsic connection between citation markers and referenced content, mitigating over-reliance on prompt format parsing</cite>.
- Causal evidence: Empirical evaluations report higher citation quality and better alignment of claims to sources under generate-then-refine and hybrid citation pipelines, indicating that training and prompt-level mechanisms causally increase appropriate citation frequency and reduce irrelevant self-attribution. <cite id="6d1bc0cf-3">A Generate-then-Refine method completes relevant citations and removes irrelevant ones without altering the response text, substantially improving correctness and citation quality on multiple datasets</cite>.

4) Grounded decoding and reference resolution shape source diversity and claim-to-source mapping
- Mechanism and effect: Multi-stage or continuous decoding that first surfaces doc IDs/mentions, then fine-grained references, then answers can reduce irrelevant redundancy and bias toward precise references. <cite id="b58d326c-4">CorpusLM decodes relevant DocIDs to documents, then decodes fine-grained references extracted from the documents, and finally decodes the answer in a single continuous process to avoid irrelevant/redundant information</cite>. Noise sampling and dual-objective training further regularize reliance on prior references. <cite id="b58d326c-4">Noise sampling replaces ground-truth references with random sentences during training to prevent over-reliance on previous references; the loss jointly optimizes reference extraction and answer generation</cite>.
- Causal evidence: Controlled ablations and training-time objectives shift the distribution of citations from repetitive or loosely grounded mentions to a more diverse set of precise references, improving factuality and verifiability. <cite id="6d1bc0cf-2">Retrieval quality, question types, and model knowledge considerably influence the trustworthiness of generated citations, with extended experiments demonstrating improved cross-scenario performance for a context-prior augmented citation generation method</cite>.

5) Trustworthiness, refusal, and attributable RAG change the willingness to cite and the base rates of unsupported claims
- Mechanism and effect: Architectures that enforce grounded attributions, learn to refuse when evidence is insufficient, and measure support degrees modulate citation frequency and conservativeness. <cite id="6d1bc0cf-2">A trustworthy citation generation paradigm that considers both internal and external knowledge introduces metrics for answer helpfulness, citation faithfulness, and trustworthiness and reports better cross-scenario performance</cite>. <cite id="6d1bc0cf-4">Mechanistic analyses show attribution drift in long-form RAG—long outputs increase the risk of misattribution—and that transformer attention submodules provide detectable internal signatures of citation hallucination</cite>. <cite id="6e9c7dbb-4">Work on attributable RAG and verifiability of long-form text, along with fine-grained evaluations of support degrees and claim granularity, indicates that grounded attributions and refusal to cite missing evidence improve trust</cite>.
- Causal evidence: Systems that integrate explicit refusal/grounding show measurable improvements in citation faithfulness and reduced hallucination influence, indicating that these control mechanisms causally increase appropriate citation and reduce unsupported citation rates. <cite id="6d1bc0cf-3">Improved citation generation mechanisms substantially enhance citation quality, including correctness and appropriateness, across multiple benchmarks</cite>.

# Mechanisms theoretically proposed or weakly empirically validated

1) Citation recommendation, attribution-as-query, and LM reranking of sources
- Mechanism and status: Treating citation search as a retrieval problem over documents and passages, with LMs used to rank candidate sources or spans by relevance; closely related to academic citation recommendation and literary evidence retrieval. <cite id="6d1bc0cf-1">Redefine source attribution as reranking candidates with the LM; attribution is similar to citation recommendation, and to evidence retrieval in literary analysis, where the goal is to retrieve the correct quoted passage given context</cite>. <cite id="6d1bc0cf-0">Studies emphasize adapting retrieval to the structure of scholarly engagement, moving from paper-level to passage-level attribution</cite>.
- Evidence: Conceptually mature and implemented in attribution/reranking modules, but broad-scale causal impact on citation base rates and diversity is still under systematic evaluation beyond targeted tasks; most studies validate retrieval quality improvements rather than end-to-end citation pattern shifts in open-domain RAG. <cite id="6d1bc0cf-1">Prior work focuses on retrieval performance rather than generation; passage-level attribution generalizes beyond direct quotation but remains complex</cite>.

2) Fair ranking and equitable exposure of sources in citations
- Mechanism and status: Fairness-aware retrieval aims to avoid bias in which sources are retrieved, which in turn changes which sources appear in outputs. <cite id="6e9c7dbb-3">Fair rankings impact ranking and generation quality and alter the equitable attribution of sources in final outputs; fairer models can maintain or surpass traditional effectiveness while improving equitable exposure of sources</cite>.
- Evidence: Strong conceptual and empirical grounding in retrieval and exposure effects, but direct measurements of downstream citation frequency distributions across demographic or venue groups in deployed RAG systems are limited. <cite id="6e9c7dbb-3">Retrieval-stage improvements translate into more equitable exposure of the sources that appear in the generated text</cite>.

3) Mechanistic attribution monitoring and internal signal detection
- Mechanism and status: Using transformer attention and hidden-state features to detect and prevent citation hallucination in long-form outputs. <cite id="6d1bc0cf-4">Transformer attention processes external context; attribution drift accumulates over long outputs; internal signatures can be measured to detect citation hallucinations</cite>.
- Evidence: Mechanistic proposals with growing empirical validation (detection tasks, long-form analyses), but closed-loop interventions that automatically correct misattributions during generation are less mature and often rely on post-hoc filtering rather than causal prevention. <cite id="6d1bc0cf-4">Detecting citation hallucinations requires a distinct approach due to their trust-amplifying effects; internal signatures provide a path to mechanistic detection</cite>.

4) Long-term citation graphs and continuous citation attribution across generations
- Mechanism and status: Systems that maintain evolving citation graphs and continuously attribute claims to sources across iterative reasoning or multi-LLM pipelines. <cite id="6d1bc0cf-1">Granular source attribution across multiple parts of a source differs from coarse paper-level citation, motivating continuous, passage-level attribution mechanisms</cite>. <cite id="b58d326c-4">Unified decoding across doc IDs and references suggests a direction toward continuous, reference-level attribution in a single pass</cite>.
- Evidence: Emerging prototypes and architectural proposals; rigorous, large-scale ablations on stability, temporal skew, and diversity of citations across multi-step tasks remain limited. <cite id="b58d326c-4">Continuous decoding of doc IDs, references, and answers with noise sampling and dual losses indicates a path to stable, reference-level attribution</cite>.

5) Prompt-level penalties/bonuses for citations and refusal policies
- Mechanism and status: Directly shaping citation behavior via rewards/penalties in decoding or explicit refusal instructions when evidence is missing. <cite id="6d1bc0cf-2">Trustworthy citation generation that considers internal and external knowledge introduces control over helpfulness, faithfulness, and trustworthiness, with retrieval quality and question type influencing outcomes</cite>.
- Evidence: Practical gains are reported in unified frameworks that learn to refuse citing unsupported content; however, standardized causal ablations isolating token-level citation penalties/bonuses in production systems are still scarce. <cite id="6d1bc0cf-4">Grounded attributions and refusal to cite missing evidence are emphasized to improve verifiability and reduce hallucinated citations</cite>.

# What changes in citation patterns, mechanism-by-mechanism

- Coverage and topicality: Better hybrid retrieval and reranking expand the relevant source set and improve precision, which increases the chance that on-topic, recent sources are cited and reduces off-topic citations. <cite id="6e9c7dbb-0">A multi-level hybrid RAG improves retrieval precision and context-aware citation generation</cite>. <cite id="6e9c7dbb-1">Hybrid dense+sparse with cross-encoder reranking provides robust evidence foundations for citation verification</cite>. <cite id="6e9c7dbb-2">Question decomposition increases retrieval coverage; reranking improves ranking precision</cite>.
- Specificity and faithfulness: Full-text grounding and citation sentence generation shift citations from paper-level tags to span-level support, increasing direct evidence alignment and reducing generic or mismatched citations. <cite id="6d1bc0cf-0">Using CTS instead of abstracts avoids hallucinations and improves contextual relevance; full-text integration is crucial</cite>. <cite id="b58d326c-0">Citation text generation with CTS and FiD aligns claims to specific source spans</cite>.
- Frequency and conservativeness: Instruction-tuned and generate-then-refine pipelines increase appropriate citation rates and reduce unnecessary/excessive or irrelevant citations by learning to add and remove references. <cite id="6d1bc0cf-3">Generate-then-Refine completes relevant citations and removes irrelevant ones, improving citation correctness and quality</cite>. <cite id="6d1bc0cf-2">Retrieval quality and model knowledge strongly affect citation trustworthiness and cross-scenario performance</cite>.
- Diversity and exposure: Fair ranking and reference-level decoding change which sources are surfaced and cited, improving equitable exposure and mitigating bias in source selection. <cite id="6e9c7dbb-3">Fair rankings improve equitable exposure of sources that appear in outputs while maintaining generation quality</cite>. <cite id="b58d326c-4">Decoding doc IDs and fine-grained references before final answers reduces redundancy and targets specific evidence</cite>.
- Long-form reliability: Mechanistic attribution monitoring detects drift and hallucinated citations, improving long-document reliability; post-hoc attribution and refusal policies curb unsupported claims and citation inflation. <cite id="6d1bc0cf-4">Attribution drift increases misattribution risk over long outputs; internal signatures can be measured for detection</cite>. <cite id="6d1bc0cf-3">Refinement mechanisms improve citation quality and reduce unnecessary or excessive citations</cite>.

# Empirically established vs. theoretically proposed

Empirically established (ablations, benchmarks, improved metrics):
- Retrieval and reranking changes: <cite id="6e9c7dbb-0">Hybrid multi-level RAG improves citation generation quality</cite>; <cite id="6e9c7dbb-1">Hybrid dense+sparse with neural reranking improves citation verification</cite>; <cite id="6e9c7dbb-2">Question decomposition and reranking ablations improve coverage and precision</cite>.
- Full-text grounding and citation sentence generation: <cite id="6d1bc0cf-0">CTS-based grounding reduces hallucinations and improves citation accuracy</cite>; <cite id="b58d326c-0">FiD-based pipelines align claims to precise spans and multiple references</cite>.
- Instruction-tuned attribution and generate-then-refine: <cite id="b58d326c-1">C$^2$-Cite instruction tuning strengthens citation-content alignment in single-pass generation</cite>; <cite id="6d1bc0cf-3">Generate-then-Refine improves citation correctness and quality across datasets</cite>.
- Trustworthiness, refusal, and attributable RAG: <cite id="6d1bc0cf-2">Context-prior augmented citation generation shows improved trustworthiness across scenarios and factors</cite>; <cite id="6e9c7dbb-4">Attributable RAG and fine-grained support evaluations validate grounded attributions and refusal policies</cite>.
- Fairness-aware retrieval and exposure: <cite id="6e9c7dbb-3">Fair rankings improve equitable exposure of sources and maintain generation quality</cite>.

Theoretically proposed or weakly validated (promising but less field-wide validation):
- Citation recommendation and attribution-as-query frameworks as primary retrieval signals. <cite id="6d1bc0cf-1">Source attribution as reranking with LMs, akin to citation recommendation and literary evidence retrieval</cite>.
- Long-term attribution drift and mechanistic detection as a basis for online correction during generation. <cite id="6d1bc0cf-4">Internal transformer signatures and attribution drift motivate detection and correction in long-form RAG</cite>.
- Unified, continuous citation attribution across multi-stage decoding and reference-level objectives. <cite id="b58d326c-4">Continuous DocIDs-References-Answer decoding with noise sampling and dual losses targets stable reference-level attribution</cite>.
- Fairness-aware citation exposure at scale in open-domain assistants. <cite id="6e9c7dbb-3">Fair rankings improve equitable source exposure, but large-scale citation distributional studies remain limited</cite>.
- Token-level citation penalties/bonuses and refusal heuristics beyond prompt-level instructions. <cite id="6d1bc0cf-2">Trustworthy citation generation emphasizes control over helpfulness and faithfulness, but standardized causal ablations of token-level citation shaping are still emerging</cite>.

# Practical implications for engineering RAG citation behavior

- To increase use of recent, on-topic sources and reduce off-topic citations, employ hybrid dense+sparse retrieval with cross-encoder reranking and, where applicable, question decomposition to expand coverage while preserving precision. <cite id="6e9c7dbb-0">Hybrid multi-level retrieval improves precision and citation generation</cite>; <cite id="6e9c7dbb-1">Dense+sparse with reranking provides robust evidence for citation verification</cite>; <cite id="6e9c7dbb-2">Decomposition and reranking jointly improve coverage and ranking quality</cite>.
- To improve faithfulness and specificity, ground generation on full-text CTS and adopt citation sentence generation with intent controls (e.g., background, method, supportive) to shape the semantic role of each citation. <cite id="6d1bc0cf-0">CTS grounding improves accuracy and avoids hallucinations</cite>; <cite id="b58d326c-3">Intent labels guide multiple-reference citation generation with controlled roles</cite>.
- To calibrate frequency and trust, tune or fine-tune attribution within in-generation pipelines (e.g., C$^2$-Cite) and add generate-then-refine modules that add or remove citations without altering claims; combine with refusal policies to avoid citing unsupported content. <cite id="b58d326c-1">Instruction-tuned attribution strengthens citation-content alignment</cite>; <cite id="6d1bc0cf-3">Refinement improves correctness and reduces unnecessary/excessive citations</cite>; <cite id="6d1bc0cf-2">Trustworthy generation considers internal and external knowledge to improve faithfulness</cite>.
- To diversify exposure and mitigate bias, integrate fairness-aware ranking and reference-level decoding to surface underrepresented sources and reduce redundant citations from irrelevant passages. <cite id="6e9c7dbb-3">Fair ranking improves equitable exposure and maintains quality</cite>; <cite id="b58d326c-4">Reference-level decoding reduces redundancy and focuses on precise evidence</cite>.
- For long-form reliability, deploy mechanistic attribution monitors that detect drift and hallucinated citations, and prefer post-hoc attribution or grounded decoding when interpretability and verifiability are paramount. <cite id="6d1bc0cf-4">Attribution drift increases misattribution risk; internal signatures enable detection</cite>; <cite id="6d1bc0cf-1">Post-hoc attribution and reranking provide interpretability but add computational cost</cite>.

Two classes of mechanisms need more head-to-head causal evidence in deployed systems: (1) prompt-level and decoding-level citation shaping (token-level penalties/bonuses, refusal heuristics) with standardized citation-level metrics, and (2) closed-loop, online attribution correction that interrupts or re-routes generation when drift is detected. <cite id="6d1bc0cf-2">Retrieval quality and model knowledge influence citation trustworthiness, yet broader causal ablations of token-level shaping are limited</cite>; <cite id="6d1bc0cf-4">Mechanistic detection of citation hallucination is established, but real-time corrective decoding is less mature and often post-hoc</cite>. Controlled, large-scale ablations that measure citation frequency, topical/temporal skew, diversity, and factuality under each mechanism would resolve remaining uncertainties and enable principled design of citation policies within RAG systems. <cite id="6d1bc0cf-3">Generate-then-Refine demonstrates gains, but generalization across domains and tasks requires broader evaluation</cite>.

# Framing the Ecosystem and the Role of Citations

Citations are a central currency in academia, shaping evaluation, funding, rankings, and the diffusion of attention and credit across actors such as authors, institutions, publishers, libraries, and users. Scholars’ actual citation decisions reflect multidimensional heuristics—proximity, authority, and inertia—with high-profile authors showing especially strong inertia (i.e., reliance on already-cited works), tying citation practices to policy and career outcomes. <cite id="210f04b2-0">Citation proximity, authority, and inertia jointly shape scholarly citation decisions, with top-h index scholars correlating citation choices most strongly with inertia</cite> <cite id="210f04b2-1">Citations influence funding allocations, academic evaluations, and university rankings, making citation analysis a core component of research evaluation and policy</cite>. In this environment, RAG systems that recommend, insert, or constrain references can alter who is seen, cited, and credited, with heterogeneous consequences across stakeholders.

# Empirical Patterns in LLM/RAG Citation Behavior

Multiple studies show that LLM-generated references and RAG-mediated recommendation already encode systematic distortions relative to human-curated baselines. Models exhibit a strong preference for highly cited works (a “Matthew effect”), favoring recent, short, low-author-count references, and in some analyses reduce self-citation relative to human patterns. <cite id="79ba4e8d-1">LLM-generated references show a strong preference for highly cited papers, reinforcing the Matthew effect, while aligning semantically with focal papers and reproducing local citation-graph properties</cite>. <cite id="79ba4e8d-3">LLMs mirror human citation patterns yet display a heightened high-citation bias that persists after controlling for year, title length, authors, and venue; they may amplify existing biases and skew dissemination</cite>. Controlled experiments further indicate that LLMs can recommend references that look plausible yet are systematically wrong or skewed, and that their topology-only regularities can mask latent selection differences. <cite id="79ba4e8d-4">LLM-generated bibliographies can match coarse bibliometric and graph-structural regularities while differing in latent selection, raising concerns that LLMs mediating scholarly discourse may distort citation networks and amplify disparities across demographics, geography, and majority/minority status</cite>.

Language and repository choices also skew outcomes. In multilingual RAG, models preferentially cite English sources—especially when query language is English—and this bias is amplified for lower-resource languages and mid-context positions, sometimes trading relevance for language preference. <cite id="2fde2272-4">Across eight languages and six models, LLMs preferentially cite English sources, with bias amplified for lower-resource languages and mid-context documents; models trade off relevance for language preference</cite>. In related-work synthesis over arXiv, systems leveraging open-access corpora and full-text grounding emphasize citation-backed accuracy and show how retrieval design shapes which works are foregrounded. <cite id="2fde2272-2">RAG systems grounded in open-access corpora like arXiv synthesize citation-backed content to mitigate hallucinations, highlighting how retrieval choices influence which sources are cited and attributed</cite>.

Importantly, RAG and generative citation mechanisms introduce new failure modes that pit verifiability against helpfulness. Requiring citations can improve accountability but undermines usefulness when evidence is insufficient for the claim, and attribution-first or post-hoc pipelines add latency and complexity. <cite id="79ba4e8d-2">Citations improve verifiability in RAG but weaken usefulness when valid responses lack sufficient evidence; attribution-first and post-hoc approaches trade off accuracy against inference cost and latency</cite>. These constraints matter because real-world RAG often compresses into fast, generative pipelines that approximate parametric knowledge, leaving structural biases uncorrected.

# Stakeholder Groups: Systematic Advantages and Disadvantages

- Senior, high-visibility authors and inertia-driven networks:
  - Advantage: Models that mirror “dominant” patterns tend to cite already-well-cited works, reinforcing momentum for established authors and venues. <cite id="79ba4e8d-1">LLM-generated references reinforce the Matthew effect by preferentially citing highly cited papers</cite> <cite id="210f04b2-0">Top-h-index scholars’ citation choices correlate most strongly with citation inertia, nearly three times stronger than for ordinary scholars</cite>.
  - Mechanism: RAG pipelines that rely on parametric priors or popularity signals amplify preexisting hub-like structures, increasing the visibility and embeddedness of already-cited clusters and affiliated authors.

- Institutions and ecosystems with strong OA and preprint infrastructures:
  - Advantage: Open and preprint-centric repositories (e.g., arXiv, institutional preprint servers) can be surfaced by RAG grounded in these corpora, enabling faster, broader initial citation and related-work synthesis—potentially accelerating impact for authors in these ecosystems. <cite id="2fde2272-2">Open-access, dynamic RAG over arXiv emphasizes citation-backed synthesis and adapts to rapid corpus growth, foregrounding OA sources</cite> <cite id="79ba4e8d-2">Post-hoc retriever-based attribution can efficiently add citations to responses, suggesting pathways to elevate OA-accessible sources</cite>.
  - Disadvantage (latent): Even when content is OA, ranking and contextual selection can still favor English-language sources and well-funded institutions, potentially marginalizing non-English and lower-resource institutional repositories. <cite id="2fde2272-4">English-language preference in citation choices is amplified for lower-resource languages and mid-context documents</cite>.

- Junior authors, interdisciplinary and HSS scholars, and small institutions:
  - Disadvantage: If RAG’s popularity signals and heuristics systematically underweight early-career or lower-impact work, visibility lags and credit accrual slows; language and repository biases can further depress citation uptake for non-English and non-OA outputs. <cite id="79ba4e8d-1">LLM-generated references reduce self-citations relative to human behavior, potentially deprioritizing internal contributions that are common in early-career and interdisciplinary work</cite> <cite id="79ba4e8d-4">LLM-mediated selection may amplify disparities across demographics, geography, and majority/minority status</cite>.
  - Structural confounds: Institutional access constraints and field-specific inequality mean OA advantages for some groups may be offset by journal prestige and language gatekeeping embedded in RAG sources. <cite id="62fbf3f5-1">Open access and preprints can act as near substitutes for paywalled versions; OA removes access barriers that drive hollow citing and bias toward accessible journals</cite> <cite id="62fbf3f5-0">Preprints exhibit higher citation inequality by affiliation than publisher versions, with twice the Gini at the institutional level, suggesting OA-only exposure can unevenly boost visibility</cite>.

- Publishers, mega-journals, and English-language scholarly cultures:
  - Advantage: Popularity-driven RAG and the preference for recent, concise, English-language sources can privilege content routed through major platforms and journals, benefiting publishers with strong indexing, discoverability, and enforcement of access/quality signals. <cite id="79ba4e8d-1">Models favor recent, shorter, fewer-author references, aligning with journal-centric, compact bibliographies</cite> <cite id="2fde2272-4">English-language bias in citations is amplified, especially in lower-resource settings</cite>.
  - Disadvantage (latent): OA mandates and commons-based infrastructures can erode traditional gatekeeping and citation concentration, exposing quality and relevance signals without profit-driven intermediaries. <cite id="62fbf3f5-4">Bibliometric studies report OA journals enjoying a 25–250% citation advantage, driven by reduced access constraints and user-driven quality selection</cite>.

- Students and early-career researchers adopting LLMs for writing:
  - Advantage: RAG-assisted reference generation can raise output quality and reduce plagiarism in drafts, improving acceptance odds if integrated well with retrieval. <cite id="79ba4e8d-0">Asking LLMs to generate proposals with citations mitigates plagiarism concerns but often results in referencing a few well-known papers; RAG and external tools are used to improve citation accuracy</cite>.
  - Disadvantage: Overreliance on a few high-profile sources and citation hallucinations can normalize misattribution and shallow literature reviews, increasing the risk of inadvertent plagiarism and reviewer burden. <cite id="79ba4e8d-0">Non-retrieval LLMs cite many hallucinated papers; even with RAG, verifying omissions requires expert work, adding to reviewer workload</cite>.

- Multilingual and non-English scholarship:
  - Disadvantage: Language preference in RAG can depress citation uptake for non-English works, even when thematically relevant; mid-context placement and lower-resource languages see stronger bias. <cite id="2fde2272-4">LLMs trade relevance for English sources, with bias amplified for lower-resource languages and mid-context documents</cite>.
  - Broader equity: Preprint and OA cultures that facilitate early sharing can partially offset language bias, but exposure and indexing inequalities persist. <cite id="62fbf3f5-2">Confounding factors like journal reputation, language, and institutional prestige can drive apparent OA advantages; delayed OA and publisher antipiracy practices can bias measured citation gains</cite>.

# Conflicting Interests and Why “Bias Amplification” Is Contested

RAG sits at the intersection of verifiability, latency, and coverage. Requiring citations improves auditability but can harm answer quality when evidence is insufficient, pushing systems toward fast, generative pipelines that may not correct structural biases. <cite id="79ba4e8d-2">Insufficient citations degrade usefulness; attribution-first and post-hoc pipelines add complexity and latency, leading to generative citation as the dominant deployment choice</cite>. This creates a trade-off between “defensibility” and “helpfulness,” where stakeholders with different incentives push the system in opposite directions: open-science advocates want broad, equitable attribution and lower barriers for non-English and preprint work; publishers and platforms value discoverability and quality curation that often privileges established venues and languages. <cite id="2fde2272-4">Language preference in citations emerges even when relevance is controlled, indicating model-driven gatekeeping that conflicts with purely informativeness-based goals</cite>.

Measurement disputes further contest the claim that RAG uniformly “amplifies bias.” First, the very mechanisms that make citation patterns look plausible can mask selection shifts, so topology-only metrics may miss latent distortions. <cite id="79ba4e8d-4">LLM-generated reference lists can match surface and network regularities while differing in latent selection, making bias detection difficult without fused semantic and structural checks</cite>. Second, OA and preprint dynamics introduce confounds: some studies attribute higher citations to OA via selection or early-view advantages, while others find an independent OA quality advantage; delayed OA and publisher policies can confound observed effects. <cite id="62fbf3f5-2">Alternative explanations for OA citation advantages include selection bias and early-view effects, with evidence that independent advantages exist but are intertwined with journal reputation and institutional factors</cite> <cite id="62fbf3f5-3">Replications show free-access articles receive more citations, but differences in hosting sites and journal practices (e.g., delayed OA, antipiracy) complicate attribution</cite>. Third, self-citation governance is itself contested: moderate self-citation is natural for continuity, yet self-citation compounds disparities over careers, motivating adjustments like SCAI; RAG can reduce self-citation, which may help or harm institutional memory and field consolidation depending on perspective. <cite id="210f04b2-1">Citations are embedded in evaluation and policy, making governance choices high-stakes</cite> <cite id="210f04b2-3">Self-citation effects are non-linear and compound over time, widening perceived impact disparities; adjustments should be field- and career-stage-aware</cite>.

Finally, disciplinary cultures and institutional policies shape outcomes. Some fields prize compact, recent bibliographies; others value long-tail, multilingual traditions. RAG’s parametric priors and retrieval corpora can skew toward compact, English, journal-centric profiles, which may align with some evaluation regimes but alienate others. <cite id="79ba4e8d-1">LLM-generated references align with compact, recent profiles and local citation-network regularities, reinforcing field-specific norms</cite> <cite id="2fde2272-4">Language preference in citations varies with query language and resource scarcity, affecting multilingual fields differently</cite>. Because stakeholders’ interests—credit allocation, discoverability, integrity, cost, and pedagogy—pull in different directions, “bias amplification” resists a single, uncontested empirical verdict; rather, it is a contested thesis whose resolution depends on which metrics, retrieval corpora, and governance goals one prioritizes.

# Toward Equitable Design: Mechanisms, Metrics, and Governance

- Retrieval governance: Prefer diverse, representative corpora (including preprints, arXiv, institutional repositories, non-English venues), multilingual indexing, and full-text grounding with relevance thresholds to mitigate language and repository biases. <cite id="2fde2272-2">Grounding in open-access corpora and full-text can improve citation-backed synthesis and reduce hallucinations</cite> <cite id="2fde2272-4">Language-aware evaluation shows English preference and mid-context underrepresentation, guiding diversity-aware retrieval design</cite>.
- Citation quality controls: Combine generative citations with post-hoc verifiers and missingness audits to reduce hallucinations and omissions without sacrificing latency. <cite id="79ba4e8d-2">Generative citation is simple and fast but prone to insufficiency; retrieval-based post-hoc attribution provides efficient baselines for completeness</cite>.
- Metric pluralism: Pair popularity- and novelty-aware signals with structural and semantic checks (embeddings, GNNs) to detect latent selection bias and avoid false “regularity” complacency. <cite id="79ba4e8d-4">Fusing network structure with semantic representations helps detect skewed LLM-generated references that look plausible but are systematically wrong or imbalanced</cite>.
- Policy alignment: Align tenure, promotion, and review workflows with open-access and preprint exposure to reduce access-driven citation bias; calibrate self-citation measures to avoid over-penalizing continuity. <cite id="62fbf3f5-1">Reducing reliance on citations as a sole quality proxy and adopting numerical systems can curb surname-order and access-driven biases</cite> <cite id="210f04b2-3">Self-citation adjustment frameworks can narrow perceived disparities while respecting field- and stage-specific norms</cite>.

# Summary

Empirically, RAG and LLMs already reshape citation selection toward highly cited, recent, English, and journal-centric sources, while reducing self-citation relative to human baselines. <cite id="79ba4e8d-1">LLM citations reinforce the Matthew effect and align with compact bibliographic norms</cite> <cite id="79ba4e8d-3">LLMs amplify high-citation bias and may skew dissemination</cite> <cite id="2fde2272-4">Language preference in citations is salient and amplified in lower-resource languages</cite>. These shifts systematically advantage established authors, English-language and OA-aligned ecosystems, and institutional infrastructures that already command visibility, while disadvantaging junior, multilingual, and preprint-dependent scholars unless retrieval and governance explicitly counteract those biases. <cite id="79ba4e8d-4">LLM mediation risks amplifying disparities across demographics and geographies</cite> <cite id="62fbf3f5-0">Preprints exhibit higher affiliation-driven inequality than publisher versions, complicating OA-only pathways to equitable credit</cite>. “Bias amplification” remains contested because verifiability-latency trade-offs, latent-selection detection, and OA/quality attribution hinge on divergent goals and metrics across stakeholders; resolving it requires pluralistic measurement, diversity-aware retrieval design, and policy reforms that decouple credit from narrow popularity signals. <cite id="79ba4e8d-2">Citations improve accountability but can reduce usefulness when evidence is insufficient, constraining bias-mitigation strategies</cite> <cite id="62fbf3f5-2">OA citation advantages are intertwined with selection, early view, and institutional factors, making causal attribution difficult</cite>.
